turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: I’m here because I can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore. At the laundry, I’ve got tickets, receipts, notes, customer jobs—all of it ends up piled together, and then I don’t know what to handle first. It’s getting hard to manage.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient reports difficulty keeping work materials and customer jobs organized and prioritizing what to handle first.

turns.doctor_question: Is this difficulty with organization and managing tasks only happening at work, or are you experiencing it in other parts of your life as well?
turns.patient_response: It’s mostly what I’m noticing at work. I mean, that’s where it’s really causing trouble—tickets, receipts, notes from the workshop, customer jobs, they all end up in one pile and then I can’t figure out what to do first. I’m not saying it never happens elsewhere, but work is the main place I’m seeing it.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes work-related difficulty organizing tickets, receipts, notes, and customer jobs, leaving them unable to prioritize what to handle first.

turns.doctor_question: How much distress or anxiety are you experiencing because of this disorganization at work?
turns.patient_response: I’m not really sure how to rate it. It bothers me because it makes the day harder and I feel pressured when things pile up, but I don’t know if I’d call it anxiety exactly. It’s just frustrating and stressful when I can’t get it sorted.

turns.doctor_question: Are you noticing any difficulties in your personal relationships due to your current situation?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, some. At the shop it’s caused tense moments with the staff and with customers when orders are late or the billing gets mixed up. That’s been hard.

And outside work, at church, I’ve stepped back from helping lead some planning because people were getting frustrated with me. I don’t like that, but it felt like I was causing more problems than helping.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself easily distracted by things around you while trying to focus on a task?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I do. Like when I’m going over the day’s dry-cleaning orders, I can start out okay, but after a few minutes my mind has wandered to the labels, or choir plans, or something I need to do at home. Then I kind of snap back and realize I missed half of what I was supposed to be checking.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports that while reviewing work orders, attention wanders after a few minutes and they miss much of what they were checking.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being distracted during a task by unrelated thoughts about labels, choir plans, and home responsibilities.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're sitting still?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I think so. If I’m in a church committee meeting or one of those fabric-care trainings, I have a hard time just staying seated. I’ll keep finding reasons to get up—get water, grab papers, check on something—even when everyone else is sitting still.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports difficulty remaining seated during meetings and trainings, repeatedly finding reasons to get up while others remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I do. I’ll jump in with an answer before someone’s even finished asking me—like my daughter, or a customer at work, or a trainer. Then sometimes I realize I answered the wrong question because I didn’t wait to hear the whole thing. It’s embarrassing.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient reports repeatedly answering before others have finished asking questions, leading to answers that do not address the full question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel like you're constantly on the go, even when you're not necessarily needing to be?
turns.patient_response: I’m not really sure. I mean, I do keep busy a lot, but I haven’t really thought of it as feeling “constantly on the go.” I guess I’d need to think about what you mean by that.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have trouble following through on instructions or finishing tasks in your personal life, like at home or with hobbies?
turns.patient_response: Yes. If somebody gives me a few things to do, I’ll usually start with the first one, and then I get pulled off into something else before I finish the rest. Like if I’m supposed to call the supplier, tag a silk blouse, and enter a receipt, I might make the call and then the other two just don’t get done unless someone reminds me.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient reports starting the first of several assigned tasks but becoming diverted and leaving the remaining tasks unfinished unless reminded.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have intense mood swings, where you quickly become very angry, excited, or upset?
turns.patient_response: I’m not sure I’d call it intense mood swings. I can get irritated or upset sometimes, like anyone, but I haven’t really noticed it changing suddenly or getting extreme.

symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient reports not noticing sudden or extreme mood changes, denying intense mood swings.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself engaging in excessive running, climbing, or other physical activities in your free time?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I don’t usually run around or climb on things or anything like that in my free time. I might keep busy, but not in that kind of way.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have difficulty sustaining focus on tasks that require mental effort over a long period of time?
turns.patient_response: Yes, I do. I can start going through the day’s dry-cleaning orders just fine, but after a few minutes my mind is somewhere else — like thinking about labels, or choir plans, or something I need to do at home. Then I’ll look back and realize I missed half of what I was supposed to be checking.

turns.patient_response: I think it’s been there a long time. Even back in grade school, my teachers would tell my mother I was bright, but scattered. I’d talk out of turn, lose papers, and need reminders to actually finish my work. So no, it’s not really new.

turns.patient_response: I’d say I first noticed it in grade school, or at least that’s when adults were pointing it out. My teachers would tell my mother I was bright, but scattered — I’d talk out of turn, lose papers, and need reminders to finish my work.

turns.patient_response: Yes, it has. At work in the laundry shop, it’s caused real problems — late orders, mixing up or confusing the billing, and then things get tense with coworkers or customers. turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced difficulties with organization, focus, or impulsivity in social situations outside of work and church?
turns.patient_response: Yes. Even outside of work and church, I’ll sometimes jump into other people’s conversations before they’re really asking me. Or if someone’s doing something, I might reach over and try to fix it myself before they ask. I know it can come off like I’m butting in, and I don’t mean it that way, but it happens.

turns.doctor_question: Were you ever diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder as a child?
turns.patient_response: I don’t think I was ever formally diagnosed as a child. If I was, nobody really told me that directly. I just remember teachers saying things to my mother, but I don’t know of any official diagnosis back then.
